messages.author: edd4914c326b6d31
messages.subject: graphical depiction of effect sizes
parts:
Not really about ggplot, but I'm hoping the folks on this list may have
some ideas. Plus, if there is a way to do it with ggplot I'd love to know.

We have estimated effects of variables on each other, both direct and
indirect effects. This is usually presented graphically with a bunch of
boxes representing variables and arrows representing effects. The
effect size and sometimes the uncertainty interval is presented as text
above the relevant line. Here's an ascii art version:
_____ 0.4 (0.2, 0.6) ______
| A | ---------------------> | B |
===== ======

meaning the effect of A on B is .4 with a confidence interval from 0.2
to 0.6. The real diagram has a lot more boxes and effects, and includes
direct and indirect effect. Often this is handled by putting the total
effect above the line and the direct effect below it.

I would like to present this graphically, probably by making the
thickness of the line proportional to the effect size, with a shaded
cloud around it indicating uncertainty.

There are a number of challenges:
* Effect sizes vary widely, from 0.5 to essentially 0. I would like
0.01 to be visually distinguishable from 0.03. Even with the
uncertainty intervals, I think most of the action is under 10%.
* If the effect is 0.4 and it ranged from -0.02 to 0.10 it is easy
enough to show the cloud of uncertainty using fainter colors (e.g.,
lower opacity). But if the lower limit is positive (as in the ascii
graph above) it is less clear to me how to present it.
* It would be useful to use color, e.g., positive effects are black and
negative ones are red), but we may be limited to black and white for
publication.
* Presenting total and direct effect information in the same arrow seems
liable to produce information overload.

Any ideas?

Thanks.
Ross Boylan

messages.author: a9413cb4eedc9e12
messages.subject: Re: graphical depiction of effect sizes
parts:
Hi Ross,
It may depend on what document processor you use. The Latex package, TikZ, will do exactly what you want and relatively easily too. However you would need to use LaTex or something like the rather nice LaTeX front end, LyX http://www.lyx.org/ (highly recommended), to use it.
I'd suggest googling for TikZ and having a look at the rather intimidating manual and the rather minimal guide, as the name says, “A very minimal introduction to Ti k Z” both available here http://www.ctan.org/pkg/pgf. For more balanced and very illustrative guide have a look at the 30 or so page “tikz pour l'impatient” which gives a better set of examples IMHO.
Even if you don't read French the examples in “tikz pour l'impatient” are very clear, show what TikZ can do and the accompanying code shows how to go about it.

messages.author: 43d45a846d16a3b9
messages.subject: Re: graphical depiction of effect sizes
parts:
These are my suggestions from a graphics practice perspective, because graphics is important for displaying effect size.

The TikZ example is ineffective. You need to have a meaningful mapping of numerical value to graphical element. Mapping to line width is very inaccurate, see Cleveland's hierarchy of visual elements. This display no better than showing a table of the numbers.

It is important to show the data, particularly when displaying effect size. My main experience is from bioinformatics examples, where there is massive multiple testing.  In bioinformatics, fold change is a popular statistic, and a measure of effect size, but on its own it is misleading. Ideally one pots the data, on a relevant scale to all the data used, along with other indicators of fold change and statistical significance. Similarly just showing p-values, even adjusted p-values, for bioinformatics is also misleading. They should be accompanied by plots of the data and the fold change.
